hero.name: Deepa
hero.who: a homemaker and new housing society secretary in Pune whose notices everyone ignores

story.b: Deepa becomes secretary of her housing society in Pune with big hopes. The garbage collectors complain that residents mix wet and dry waste. The terrace water tank overflows often. Maintenance payments arrive late. Deepa does what everyone does. She prints posters for the lift, sends long WhatsApp messages and gives a speech at the annual meeting. Everyone nods and agrees. Nothing changes. Two weeks later, the bins are as mixed as ever, and the man from B wing who clapped loudest at her speech is seen throwing a plastic bag into the wet bin. Deepa sits at home with her filter coffee, frustrated. People clearly know what to do. So why do they not do it?

ask.q: Residents agree with Deepa but do not change their habits. What should she try next?
o: Print bigger, stricter posters with warnings
Look at how the choices are set up and make the right one easier
Give up, since people never change
ask.why: Bigger posters repeat what already failed, and giving up ignores a real lever. People often know the right thing but act on habit and convenience. Changing how choices are presented, so the good option is also the easy one, often works better than more instructions.

chapters.take: Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it.

story.b: Before blaming anyone, Deepa notices something about herself. She has planned to cut her electricity bill for months. Yet every afternoon she switches on the AC when the fan would do, simply because the remote is right there. Last week she planned to save for a family trip, then spent the money in an online sale she spotted at midnight. She is not a careless person. She is just human. The same is true of her neighbours, she realises. At 8 am they are rushing to work, carrying a child, a tiffin and a bag of garbage. Nobody stops to sort plastic in that moment. Deepa sees that the gap between plan and action is not laziness. It is ordinary life.

ask.q: A committee member says residents who do not segregate are simply irresponsible. What is the more useful view?
o: Agree, and publish the names of those who do not comply
Assume residents will improve once they read the rules again
Accept that busy people act on habit, and design for how they really behave
ask.why: Shaming makes people defensive, and repeating rules assumes everyone behaves like a perfect calculator, which nobody does. People get rushed, distracted and swayed by convenience. Designing for how humans actually behave gives Deepa a real chance to close the gap between plans and actions.

chapters.take: People are not perfectly rational. Plan for real humans.

story.b: Deepa walks the path a resident takes each morning, from the lift to the gate. One big bin stands right beside the lift, so everything goes into it. The small dry-waste bin is hidden behind the parking, near the watchman's cabin. Nobody walks there with a child and a bag on a rushed morning. The setup was never neutral. It was quietly pushing everyone to mix their waste. So Deepa asks the watchman to place a green bin and a blue bin side by side next to the lift, each with a picture showing what goes in. She removes the single big bin. Nobody gets a lecture. In the first week, the garbage collector notices the difference and smiles for the first time.

ask.q: Deepa wants more residents to use the new society library shelf. Which change will probably help most?
o: Place the shelf where people already pass, like near the lift
Keep it in the clubhouse but send more reminders
Ask residents to promise they will visit weekly
ask.why: Reminders and promises depend on people going out of their way, which they rarely do. Where something is placed quietly shapes what people choose. Putting the shelf on the path they already walk makes borrowing a book the easy, natural option.

chapters.take: There is no neutral design. Arrange choices so the good one is easy.

story.h: A green bucket at every door
story.b: Deepa wants residents to compost their kitchen waste. Last year, the society asked people to sign up for composting, and only six flats did. This time she changes the starting point. Every flat gets a small green compost bucket delivered to its door, with a friendly note explaining how to use it. Anyone who does not want it can simply return it to the watchman, no questions asked. A month later, only nine of the hundred and twenty flats have returned their buckets. Most people did not actively decide to compost. They just did not decide to stop. Deepa realises that whatever is already set up tends to become what most people end up doing.

ask.q: The society wants more residents to get bills by email instead of paper. Which approach respects choice and works best?
o: Ask interested residents to fill a long form to switch
Stop paper bills completely without asking anyone
Make email the default, with an easy option to keep paper
ask.why: A long sign-up form means most people never switch, simply because doing nothing is easier. Removing paper completely takes away choice and annoys people. Making email the default while keeping an easy way back uses the power of defaults without forcing anyone.

chapters.take: Most people stick with the default, so choose defaults with care.

story.b: At the committee meeting, Mr Kulkarni wants a five-hundred-rupee fine for anyone who mixes waste, and a ban on carrying garbage bags in the lift. Others agree loudly. Deepa listens, then suggests something gentler. A short WhatsApp reminder the night before dry-waste pickup. A thank-you board at the gate each month, listing the wings with the cleanest bins. Nobody is banned or fined, and everyone is still free to do as they like. Mr Kulkarni grumbles that it is too soft, but he agrees to try it for two months. The reminder costs nothing. B wing, competitive as always, starts checking its own bins so that it can top the board.

ask.q: Mr Kulkarni says only fines will change behaviour. How should Deepa respond?
o: Agree, since people only respond to punishment
Propose reminders and gentle encouragement that keep everyone free to choose
Drop the waste issue to avoid conflict
ask.why: Fines and bans may force compliance, but they create resentment and take away freedom. Dropping the issue helps nobody. Reminders and friendly recognition steer people toward the better choice while leaving every option open, which is the heart of a respectful nudge.

chapters.take: A gentle push that keeps people free often works better than force.

story.b: The water tank on the terrace still overflows twice a week. Each time, someone forgot to switch off the pump, and hundreds of litres pour down the side of the building. People get blamed, but it keeps happening. Deepa accepts that people will always forget. So she designs for it. The society fits an automatic cut-off that stops the pump when the tank is full. Next to the switch, she adds a small red light that glows while the pump runs, so anyone passing notices. For maintenance, she prints the society's own QR code, showing its full name, on every bill, so payments stop going to the wrong account. Mistakes simply become harder to make.

ask.q: Residents often leave the terrace door unlocked at night. What would help most?
o: Fit a self-closing latch so the door locks on its own
Send a weekly message asking everyone to be more careful
Fine whoever left it open last
ask.why: Weekly reminders fade, and fines punish a mistake that anyone could make. Good systems expect human forgetfulness and make errors harder. A self-closing latch fixes the problem every single time, without anyone needing to remember anything.

chapters.take: Expect mistakes, and design so they are hard to make.

story.h: Two bins and a red light
story.b: Weeks later, the garbage collector tells Deepa that her society now has the cleanest bins on his whole route. The tank has not overflowed once since the cut-off went in. Most flats still use their green buckets, and the compost pit behind the parking smells of earth, not rubbish. Maintenance payments arrive on time, mostly through the QR code. Mr Kulkarni, to everyone's surprise, proposes a thank-you board for saving water. Deepa has not printed a single new poster. When a neighbour asks for her secret, she just points at the two bins by the lift and the little red light on the terrace. Small design choices, she says, did more than all her speeches.

chapters.take: Better design helps people do the right thing without being forced.
